title: About 3 in 100
text:
About 3 in 100.

That's roughly how often a LinkedIn application leads to an interview, according to Huntr's 2025 job search data.

The other 97 sit in a pile.

For nine years my job was getting strangers to reply. I built SDR teams at ClickUp and Deel, and a partner pipeline program at Google. The work is simple to say and hard to do: find the person who owns the problem, say something relevant, and follow up.

Nobody in sales waits for a lead form to fill itself. Job seekers are told to do exactly that.

So I built Day60: a free 60-day sprint that runs the SDR playbook on a job search. Paste a job link and it finds the four people closest to the hire and their verified work emails, then drafts your first note. You send it.

Try it on one job, no account: https://lnkd.in/gecGE9b8

Stop applying. Start prospecting.

title: Every job has four people
text:
Every open job has four people who decide if you get it.

1. The hiring manager. Owns the problem.
2. Their boss. Owns the budget and the headcount.
3. A future teammate. Can say "talk to this person."
4. The recruiter. Runs the process.

Most applicants reach one of the four. Through a form.

In sales we call that single-threaded. It's how deals die. It's how applications die too.

Go multi-threaded: four people, four short notes, each about what that person cares about.

Which of the four do you skip most?

P.S. Paste any job link at getday60.com/try. Day60 helps you identify all four, finds their verified work emails and drafts your first note.

title: Two messages, same job
text:
Two messages. Same job.

A: "I'm very passionate about this opportunity and believe I'd be a great fit."

B: "Your posting says onboarding has to get faster before the Q1 launch. At my last company I cut ours from 3 weeks to 9 days. Worth 15 minutes next week?"

A is about you. B is about them.

A could go to any company on earth. B could only go to one.

Hiring managers can tell which is which before they finish the first line.

Before you hit send, ask one question: could I paste this into another company's inbox without changing a word? If yes, rewrite it.

P.S. @Day60 drafts notes like B for each of the four people on a job, finds their verified work emails and checks every draft before you see it. Free. Link in the first comment.

title: Before sales, the ministry story
text:
Before sales, I spent nearly 10 years in ministry. Five of them as an ordained pastor.

People are surprised when I tell them that. They shouldn't be.

Every week I led from a stage. And I regularly sat with people going through the hardest parts of their lives.

So when I became an SDR and had to cold call VPs and C-suite execs, I wasn't afraid. It was just like talking to any other person.

Ministry gave me one more thing: conviction. At every company I joined, I looked for something about the work I believed in, so I could carry conviction into every cold call. It worked.

The line I usually use: "I figured I'd been 'selling' Jesus for 10 years, I might as well sell some software."

Eight years in sales later, I'm building Day60, a job-search sprint that gets you to the people who decide.

If you're changing careers, you're not starting from zero. You're bringing something most applicants don't have. Find the person who needs it and tell them, plainly.

What did your first career teach you that you still use?

title: Most job searches are single-threaded
text:
Most job searches are single-threaded.

In sales, a deal with only one contact is called single-threaded. Everyone in sales knows how those go. One person gets busy, and the whole deal goes quiet.

A job search usually runs the same way. One application, one recruiter, one inbox. If that recruiter is buried this week, so are you.

Every job has four people who shape the hire:
The hiring manager, who feels the empty seat.
Their boss, who approved the role.
Someone on the team who knows what the job really needs.
The recruiter, who runs the process.

You don't have to write to all four on day one. But know who they are, and make sure the hiring manager hears from you directly, in a short note about their team.

That's the method I built Day60 around: one job, four people, a few well-researched messages, and you send every one.
